item.title: A General-Purpose Adaptable Foundation Model for Total-Body PET Kinetic Modelling
item.description: arXiv:2610.41093v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Voxel-level kinetic modeling in total-body dynamic positron emission tomography (TB-PET) enables precise physiological quantification but complicates parameter uncertainty estimation. While generative consistency models (CMs) can rapidly estimate Bayesian posterior distributions, they are constrained by type of tracers, kinetic models, and protocols. Training them from scratch whenever a new tracer, model or protocol is used can be computationally intensive. To address this, we introduce LoRACM, a parameter-efficient framework utilizing low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to transfer a pretrained foundation CM to novel TB-PET scenarios. We evaluated three adaptation scenarios using simulated and human data: scanner and protocol transfer for FDG two-tissue compartment modeling; FP-CIT simplified reference tissue modeling; and high-temporal-resolution FDG blood flow imaging via the adiabatic approximation to tissue homogeneity model. Each adaptation was trained in less than 3 hours on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU using 50,000 simulated pairs. In simulations, LoRACM showed strong agreement with results from Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC, which we use as reference posterior distributions), yielding median Kullback-Leibler divergences of 0.05-0.11 and median absolute percentage errors below 1.2% for each kinetic parameter of interest. In human data, LoRACM generated total-body K_i maps comparable to the ones made by non-negative nonlinear least squares (NNLS) fitting and a consistency model trained from scratch. Striatal dopamine binding potential estimates predicted by LoRACM correlated with NNLS estimates (r = 0.968-0.988). LoRACM produced total-body blood flow imaging with FDG matching the one made by NNLS. These underscore the potential of adapting a pretrained CM with LoRA for fast and reliable posterior parameter inference for kinetic models across distinct TB-PET applications.

item.title: Roadmap: Image reconstruction in emission tomography for the era of fast Monte Carlo simulation
item.description: arXiv:2610.41583v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantitative image reconstruction in positron emission tomography and single photon emission computed tomography depends on how accurately the forward model describes photon emission, transport and detection. Monte Carlo simulation is the most complete model available, yet it is mostly used as an offline reference rather than inside the reconstruction. This roadmap asks what it would take to change that. The main obstacle is not only simulation time. Iterative reconstruction requires the expectation of the measured data and the gradient of the data fidelity, whereas Monte Carlo simulation produces noisy realisations of a complete acquisition. GPU implementations, variance reduction and learned surrogate models have made simulations much faster. At the same time, modern scanners acquire ever larger data sets with larger system models, and further gains in quantitative accuracy require more detailed physics. We discuss how fast Monte Carlo simulation can improve the modelling of the system response, scatter, positron range and the joint estimation of activity and attenuation, how noisy simulations can enter reconstruction algorithms, and which computing hardware makes this feasible. Monte Carlo simulation is most valuable where analytic models fail, and most practical solutions will combine both. The most immediate benefit of fast simulators is the validation and calibration of faster analytic models, together with more accurate, absolutely quantitative scatter estimates. Key open problems are the use of noisy simulations as expectations, in particular for sparse data, the computation of gradients and adjoints, the allocation of a limited simulation budget, and the use of scattered events as a source of information rather than a nuisance. Faster simulators are necessary but not sufficient, and progress requires simulators and reconstruction methods to be developed together.

item.title: Quantitative Ultrasound Characterizes Perfusion Trajectories in Healthy and Inflamed Gingival Wound Healing
item.description: arXiv:2610.41897v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rationale and Objectives: Visual examination of extraction-site healing provides limited insight into underlying vascular recovery. We developed a quantitative ultrasound framework to assess gingival perfusion and persistent inflammation. Materials and Methods: Patients (n = 51) undergoing extraction and socket preservation were imaged longitudinally using color-flow ultrasound and laser speckle contrast analysis (LASCA) from 2 weeks to 3 months after extraction. Pre-scan-converted Total Recall Imaging (TRI) data with phase information were processed using scan conversion, bilateral filtering, and power estimation to derive velocity-weighted color pixel density (CPDvel). Gingival regions of interest were automatically segmented using deep learning and assessed with Dice and Bland-Altman analyses. CPDvel was compared between healthy and inflamed visits in early (<35 days) and recovery (>35 days) periods and with LASCA. Results: Segmentation achieved a mean Dice score of 0.98 and median of 0.99 (IQR, 0.98-0.99), with minimal area bias (-0.005%; 95% limits of agreement, -1.68% to 1.67%). Median CPDvel decreased by 81% between early and recovery periods in healthy visits (p = 0.01), compared with a nonsignificant 26% reduction in inflamed visits (p = 0.31). During recovery, CPDvel was higher in inflamed than healthy visits (0.12 vs 0.03 cm/s; p = 0.04). LASCA showed smaller reductions (13% and 9%, respectively). CPDvel was positively correlated with LASCA in healthy (one-sided p = 0.03) and inflamed visits (one-sided p = 0.13). Conclusions: TRI-based quantitative ultrasound enabled automated perfusion assessment with reduced dependence on scanner display settings. Distinct perfusion patterns and more pronounced temporal changes than LASCA support its potential for noninvasive monitoring of oral wound healing and persistent inflammation.
item.dc:creator: Haowei Tai, Oscar Duran-Garnica, Karen Villarreal, Hsun-Liang Chan, Oliver D. Kripfgans

item.title: Comparison of melanin subtypes using pump-probe microscopy
item.description: arXiv:2610.40969v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Pump-probe microscopy (PPM) is used to probe excited state dynamics of endogenous chromophores to generate contrast that is unavailable in traditional forms of microscopy. Here we apply PPM to characterize melanin, a pigment central to photoprotection, skin and eye pigmentation, and melanoma pathogenesis. Melanin is notoriously difficult to analyze due to its structural and chemical complexity. We imaged melanin from six different lesion categories: cutaneous nevi, lentigo, cutaneous malignant melanoma, conjunctival melanocytic lesions, vulvar melanocytic lesions, and a murine melanoma model, across 21 independent biological samples and 109 regions of interest. Using model fitting, adapted phasor analysis, and support vector machine classification, we characterize and quantify excited-state dynamics as a surrogate for chemical and structural heterogeneity. Heterogeneity of melanin separates cutaneous from non-cutaneous lesions, but is not correlated with malignancy. Benign lentigo is the most heterogeneous population in the dataset, exceeding cutaneous malignant melanoma, while conjunctival lesions are the most homogeneous despite receiving direct solar exposure. Classification on full transient absorption curves separates most subtypes well above the six-class chance level. These findings demonstrate the ability of PPM to reveal subtle differences in melanin photophysics across diverse tissue environments, with implications for optical tissue classification and the understanding of melanoma pathogenesis.
item.dc:creator: Emma Bao, David Grass, Martin C. Fischer, Warren S. Warren
